title: Strange Scaffold's Xalavier Nelson, Jr. on picking projects for impact
summary: Unity talks to prolific indie dev Xalavier Nelson Jr. about how the Strange Scaffold studio setup helps to power indie creators and communities, and shares the DIDIT system for evaluating new projects and features for maximum impact.
body_markdown:
A project at Strange Scaffold does not start unless I have a business case for it. I need to know what type of player it's for, I know how long we're gonna develop it, what our budget is going to be, what the narrative arc is, what I need for the aesthetic and the gameplay loop... I have this entire arc of what the game is and what it fulfills for our players and for our team.


Describing my internal algorithm recently, I came to this acronym I call DIDIT: Direction, Impact, Dependencies, Iteration, and Time. I'm measuring any potential feature or decision against these five factors to figure out if something is worth doing, and whether it accomplishes the goals for our project and what it brings to players in the process.


My favorite comparison is that it's a “should” button – because there's a lot of can buttons. You can always put another thing into a game.. The advent of generative AI gives people a lot tools to say *can* , but there are precious few that are helping you find the answer to *should* . And when you, with a DIDIT-style approach, are looking at whether a feature elevates the game and suits the team, that precision means you can bring players genuinely necessary things in a way that's both effective and sustainable.


I choose Unity because it allows me to empower the people I work with to do work in a way that makes more sense for them. They get to build the tool sets they believe in, they get to choose even the version of Unity and the rendering pipeline of Unity that best suits the goals of our project, and we get to just focus on creation rather than anything else.


No one is imposing a standard way to build things on us, or making it harder for us to explore new horizons. or If I'm not making games that are typically in a genre, I don't have to bend and break the framework of the system to be able to create work that I believe in and that my players will love.


Unity lets me look at a game concept and really figure out how to build, from the ground up, the tooling and development approach that lets the game and team become the best versions of themselves.
